questions.q: In Mattingly's master equation for T_SL/W_TO, what does α represent?
questions.a: Installed thrust lapse T/T_SL at the condition
w: Instantaneous weight fraction W/W_TO at the segment
Ratio of specific excess power to installed thrust
Fraction of maximum throttle used at the condition
questions.x: α is the installed thrust lapse T/T_SL, which captures how thrust varies with altitude, Mach, and throttle schedule; β = W/W_TO is the weight fraction.

questions.q: The master equation is derived from which governing statement?
questions.a: Energy balance: (T−D)V/W = d/dt(h + V²/2g)
w: Moment balance about the aircraft center of gravity
Momentum balance across the engine control volume
Lift equals weight in every mission segment
questions.x: Specific excess power (T−D)V/W equals the rate of change of energy height h + V²/2g, and dividing by V and substituting T = αT_SL, W = βW_TO gives the master equation.

questions.q: On a T_SL/W_TO vs W_TO/S constraint diagram, the stall and landing constraints usually appear as:
questions.a: Vertical lines setting a maximum wing loading
w: Vertical lines setting a minimum wing loading
Horizontal lines setting a minimum thrust loading
Curves that rise steeply at high wing loading
questions.x: Stall and landing fix W/S ≤ ½ρV²C_Lmax independent of T/W, giving vertical lines with the feasible region to their left.

questions.q: Where is the design point usually chosen within the feasible region?
questions.a: Lowest feasible T/W, at the highest W/S there
w: Highest T/W in the region, to keep thrust margin
Lowest W/S in the region, for maximum stall margin
Centroid of the region, to balance all constraints
questions.x: The design point sits at the lowest feasible thrust loading, taking the highest wing loading available there, which gives a small engine and a small, light wing.

questions.q: The cruise constraint curve has a minimum (bucket) in T_SL/W_TO at the wing loading where:
questions.a: Parasite and induced terms are equal: C_L = √(C_D0/K)
w: The induced term equals the climb term (1/V)dh/dt
W/S equals the stall-limited maximum wing loading
The thrust lapse α reaches its peak at cruise altitude
questions.x: The bucket occurs where qC_D0/(βW/S) equals Kβ(W/S)/q, which is the maximum L/D condition C_L = √(C_D0/K).

questions.q: For a catapult launch, the aircraft's airspeed at the end of the stroke equals:
questions.a: Catapult end speed plus wind over deck
w: Catapult end speed minus wind over deck
Wind over deck alone, since the stroke is short
Catapult end speed times the thrust lapse α
questions.x: Airspeed at launch is catapult end speed plus wind over deck (ship speed plus natural wind), and it must reach the required minimum flying speed.

questions.q: For a fixed field length, a steady headwind at takeoff moves the takeoff constraint curve:
questions.a: Lower: less T/W is needed at each W/S
w: Higher: more T/W is needed at each W/S
To a vertical line at the stall wing loading
Left: a lower maximum W/S at every T/W
questions.x: A headwind lowers groundspeed at the same liftoff airspeed, shortening the roll, so the required T/W at each W/S drops and the feasible region grows.

questions.q: Put the constraint analysis steps in order
steps: Define mission requirements: field length, turn, climb, speed
Write each requirement as T_SL/W_TO vs W_TO/S via the master equation
Plot all curves and identify the feasible region
Select the design point and carry T/W and W/S into sizing
questions.x: Requirements become master equation constraints, their plot defines the feasible region, and the chosen point (T/W, W/S) feeds weight sizing.

questions.q: Stall speed at load factor n for weight W, wing area S and C_Lmax is:
questions.a: V_s = √(2nW/(ρ S C_Lmax))
w: V_s = √(nW/(2ρ S C_Lmax))
V_s = √(2W/(nρ S C_Lmax))
V_s = 2nW/(ρ S C_Lmax)
questions.x: From nW = ½ρV²SC_Lmax, stall speed is V_s = √(2nW/(ρSC_Lmax)), so it grows with √n and √(W/S).

questions.q: With drag polar C_D = C_D0 + KC_L², jet maximum range (constant TSFC) occurs at:
questions.a: C_D0 = 3KC_L², at max √C_L/C_D
w: C_D0 = KC_L², at max C_L/C_D
3C_D0 = KC_L², at max C_L^{3/2}/C_D
C_D0 = 2KC_L², at max C_L²/C_D
questions.x: Jet range scales with V(L/D) ∝ √C_L/C_D, which peaks when C_D0 = 3KC_L², at a speed 3^(1/4) ≈ 1.32 times the minimum drag speed.

questions.q: Match each flight goal to its optimum condition (polar C_D = C_D0 + KC_L²)
questions.x: Jet endurance and prop range both peak at max L/D, where C_D0 = KC_L²; prop endurance peaks at minimum power, 3C_D0 = KC_L², at 0.76 times the minimum drag speed.

questions.q: In level flight power required P_R = DV, the parasite and induced power terms scale as:
questions.a: Parasite ∝ V³, induced ∝ 1/V
w: Parasite ∝ V², induced ∝ 1/V²
Parasite ∝ V³, induced ∝ V
Parasite ∝ V, induced ∝ 1/V³
questions.x: Parasite drag grows with V² and induced drag falls with 1/V², so multiplying by V gives parasite power ∝ V³ and induced power ∝ 1/V.

questions.q: In a level coordinated turn at bank angle φ = 60°, the load factor and turn radius are:
questions.x: n = 1/cos 60° = 2 and R = V²/(g√(n²−1)) = V²/(g tan φ) = V²/(g√3).

questions.q: To first order, takeoff ground roll scales as:
questions.a: (W/S) / (ρ C_Lmax (T/W))
w: (T/W) / (ρ C_Lmax (W/S))
(W/S)² / (ρ C_Lmax (T/W))
(W/S) / (ρ² C_Lmax (T/W))
questions.x: Ground roll grows with wing loading and falls with thrust loading, density, and C_Lmax: s_G ∝ (W/S)/(ρ C_Lmax (T/W)).

questions.q: An aircraft takes off into a 20 kt headwind. Compared with calm air:
questions.a: Same liftoff airspeed, shorter ground roll
w: Lower liftoff airspeed, same ground roll
Same liftoff groundspeed, shorter ground roll
Higher stall airspeed, longer ground roll
questions.x: Stall and liftoff speeds are airspeed properties set by W/S and C_Lmax; a headwind lowers the groundspeed needed at liftoff, so the ground roll shrinks.

questions.q: The Breguet range equation for a jet (TSFC c on a weight basis) is:
questions.a: R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W_i/W_f)
w: R = (V/c)(L/D)(W_i − W_f)
R = (1/c)(L/D) ln(W_i/W_f)
R = (V/c)(D/L) ln(W_f/W_i)
questions.x: Integrating dR = −(V L/D)/(cW) dW at constant V, L/D, and c gives R = (V/c)(L/D) ln(W_i/W_f), so range grows with V(L/D)/c.

questions.q: The positive stall boundary on a V-n diagram is:
questions.a: n = ρV²SC_Lmax/(2W)
w: n = 2W/(ρV²SC_Lmax)
n = ρVSC_Lmax/(2W)
n = ρV²SC_Lmax/W
questions.x: Maximum lift ½ρV²SC_Lmax divided by weight gives the largest available load factor, a parabola in V.

questions.q: Stall speed at n = 1 is V_S1 and the positive limit load factor is 4. The maneuver (corner) speed V_A is:
questions.a: 2 V_S1
w: 4 V_S1
questions.x: V_A = V_S1√n_max = V_S1√4 = 2V_S1, where the stall parabola meets the limit load line.

questions.q: Two aircraft meet the same gust at the same EAS with equal lift-curve slope and gust alleviation factor. B has twice A's wing loading. B's gust Δn is:
questions.a: Half that of A
w: Twice that of A
Equal to that of A
Four times that of A
questions.x: Gust load increment Δn = ρ₀U_de V_e a K_g/(2W/S) scales as 1/(W/S), so heavier wing loading gives a proportionally smaller Δn.

questions.q: If the positive limit load factor is 3.8, the ultimate load factor is:
questions.x: Ultimate load equals 1.5 times limit load, so 1.5 × 3.8 = 5.7.

questions.q: Why is a V-n diagram usually plotted against equivalent airspeed?
questions.a: q = ½ρ₀V_e², so one stall curve fits all altitudes
w: EAS equals true airspeed at every altitude band
EAS removes aircraft weight from the load terms
EAS equals groundspeed, which sets the gust timing
questions.x: Aerodynamic loads depend on dynamic pressure q = ½ρ₀V_e², so plotting in EAS lets one stall boundary serve all altitudes.

questions.q: What does the corner point of the V-n diagram represent physically?
questions.a: Lowest speed that reaches the limit load factor
w: Highest speed at which the aircraft stalls at 1 g
Speed where the gust and maneuver lines cross n = 1
Speed of maximum level flight thrust at sea level
questions.x: At the corner speed V_A the stall boundary meets the limit load line, which also gives the maximum instantaneous turn rate.

questions.q: Gust lines on a V-n diagram (from the gust load equation) are:
questions.a: Straight lines from n = 1 at V = 0, slope ∝ U_de
w: Parabolas from n = 0 with curvature ∝ U_de
Horizontal lines at n = 1 ± U_de/V_C
Straight lines from n = 0 at V = 0, slope ∝ 1/U_de
questions.x: Δn grows linearly with EAS and gust velocity U_de, so gust lines radiate from n = 1 at zero speed.

questions.q: Put the steps for constructing a V-n diagram in order
steps: Plot positive and negative stall curves n = ±ρV²SC_Lmax/(2W)
Draw the limit load lines at n_max and n_min
Mark V_A at the stall and limit line intersection, then V_C and V_D
Overlay gust lines and take the outer envelope
questions.x: Stall curves and limit loads give the maneuver envelope, V_D closes it on the right, and the gust lines extend it where they exceed the maneuver loads.

questions.q: The ideal Brayton cycle consists of:
questions.a: 2 isentropic and 2 isobaric processes
w: 2 isentropic and 2 isothermal processes
2 isothermal and 2 isobaric processes
2 isentropic and 2 isochoric processes
questions.x: Ideal Brayton has isentropic compression and expansion with isobaric heat addition and rejection.

questions.q: Match each station number to its location (Mattingly / ARP 755 numbering)
questions.x: Core stations run 0 freestream, 2 fan face, 3 compressor exit, 4 turbine inlet, 5 turbine exit, 9 nozzle exit; the bypass stream uses 13 fan exit and 19 bypass nozzle exit.

questions.q: For an exhaust to flight velocity ratio V_e/V_0 = 2, ideal propulsive efficiency is:
Why does a high bypass turbofan have high propulsive efficiency?
questions.a: Large ṁ at small ΔV gives the thrust with higher η_p
w: Small ṁ at large ΔV gives the thrust with higher η_p
Bypass air raises turbine inlet temperature and work
Bypass air raises nozzle exit pressure above ambient
questions.x: Thrust is ṁΔV while wasted kinetic energy scales as ṁΔV², so moving a large mass flow with a small velocity increment raises η_p.

questions.q: What primarily limits the specific thrust a turbojet core cycle can deliver?
questions.a: Turbine inlet temperature T_t4 (materials, cooling)
w: Compressor exit temperature, set by the fuel type
Nozzle exit pressure, set by the ambient pressure
Inlet pressure recovery, set by the takeoff conditions
questions.x: Specific thrust rises with T_t4, and the maximum T_t4 is fixed by turbine material limits and cooling technology.

questions.q: Why do modern engines use two or three spools?
questions.a: Each spool runs at its own best speed, easing stall
w: All spools share one speed, shrinking the turbine
Spools let the burner run at a lower fuel-air ratio
Spools raise the nozzle exit pressure above ambient
questions.x: Separate shafts let the low and high pressure compressors each turn at their best speed, improving stall margin and stage matching over a wide range.

questions.q: Uninstalled thrust of a single-stream engine (fuel mass flow neglected) is:
questions.a: F = ṁ(V_e − V_0) + (p_e − p_0)A_e
w: F = ṁ(V_e + V_0) + (p_e − p_0)A_e
F = ṁ(V_e − V_0) − (p_e − p_0)A_e
F = ṁV_e + (p_0 − p_e)A_0
questions.x: Thrust equals momentum flux change ṁ(V_e − V_0) plus the pressure thrust (p_e − p_0)A_e at the nozzle exit.

questions.q: Which relation combines the first and second laws for a simple compressible substance?
questions.a: dh = T ds + v dp
w: dh = T ds − v dp
du = T ds + p dv
dh = s dT + v dp
questions.x: With h = u + pv and du = T ds − p dv, the Gibbs relation is dh = T ds + v dp, so along an isobar heat added equals Δh.

questions.q: The Kutta-Joukowski theorem gives lift per unit span as:
questions.a: L' = ρ∞V∞Γ
w: L' = ½ρ∞V∞²Γ
L' = ρ∞Γ/V∞
L' = ρ∞V∞²Γ
questions.x: Sectional lift equals freestream density times freestream speed times circulation Γ = ∮V·ds.

questions.q: For AR = 8, e = 0.8, and C_L = 0.5, the induced drag coefficient is about:
Holding lift, dynamic pressure, and e fixed, doubling wingspan b multiplies induced drag force by:
questions.x: D_i = L²/(π q b² e), so induced drag force depends on span loading and scales as 1/b².

questions.q: An elliptic spanwise lift distribution gives:
questions.a: Minimum induced drag for given lift and span
w: Minimum root bending moment for given lift and span
Maximum C_Lmax for a given planform area
Minimum wave drag for a given volume
questions.x: Elliptic loading produces uniform downwash and e = 1, the minimum induced drag for a given lift and span.

questions.q: Flying faster at fixed altitude (subsonic, compressibility negligible), C_D0 and parasite drag force:
questions.a: C_D0 about constant; qSC_D0 grows as V²
w: C_D0 grows as V²; qSC_D0 grows as V⁴
C_D0 falls as 1/V²; qSC_D0 stays constant
Both C_D0 and qSC_D0 stay about constant
questions.x: C_D0 is the zero-lift drag coefficient, roughly fixed by geometry and Reynolds number, while parasite drag force qSC_D0 grows with dynamic pressure and reference area.

questions.q: The wing root bending moment from a spanwise lift distribution L'(y) is:
questions.a: M_root = ∫₀^{b/2} L'(y) y dy
w: M_root = ∫₀^{b/2} L'(y) dy
M_root = ∫₀^{b/2} L'(y) y² dy
M_root = (b/2)∫₀^{b/2} L'(y) dy
questions.x: Each spanwise lift element L'(y)dy acts at moment arm y about the root, so M_root = ∫₀^{b/2} L'(y) y dy.

questions.q: Physically, how does a well designed winglet reduce induced drag?
questions.a: It raises effective span, cutting downwash at set lift
w: It adds wetted area, which raises e directly and fully
It blocks the tip vortex entirely, so downwash vanishes
It raises C_D0, trading parasite drag for wave drag
questions.x: A winglet increases the effective span of the trailing vortex system, which reduces downwash and the induced drag for the same lift.

questions.q: The drag divergence Mach number M_dd is where:
questions.a: C_D rises steeply from wave drag (dC_D/dM = 0.1)
w: Local flow first reaches sonic speed on the airfoil
Freestream flow first reaches Mach 1 on the airframe
Shock-induced separation makes C_L reach C_Lmax
questions.x: Above the critical Mach number, shocks grow and wave drag drives a steep rise in C_D, commonly defined at dC_D/dM = 0.1.

questions.q: In momentum theory for a hovering rotor, the induced velocity at the disk is:
w: v_i = T/(2ρA)
questions.x: Momentum theory gives T = 2ρA v_i², so v_i = √(T/(2ρA)), with the far wake moving at 2v_i.

questions.q: Ideal induced power in hover is:
w: P = T²/(2ρA)

questions.q: At fixed thrust and density, doubling rotor disk area multiplies ideal hover power by:
questions.x: Ideal power scales as 1/√A at fixed T and ρ, so doubling A gives 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 times the power; lower disk loading means higher hover efficiency.

questions.q: Rotor figure of merit is defined as:
questions.a: Ideal induced power divided by actual power
w: Actual power divided by ideal induced power
Thrust divided by actual shaft power
Induced power divided by profile power
questions.x: Figure of merit FM = P_ideal/P_actual, typically 0.7 to 0.8 for a good hovering rotor.

questions.q: For a helicopter, total power required versus forward speed is:
questions.a: High at hover, dips at mid speed, rises again
w: Lowest at hover, then rising steadily with speed
Peaks at mid speed, lowest at high speed
Flat to cruise speed, then rising with V³
questions.x: Induced power falls as forward speed adds mass flow through the disk, while parasite power grows as V³, giving a bucket at moderate speed.

questions.q: To hover with the same thrust and ideal power in an atmosphere with 1/60 of Earth's density, disk area must be:
questions.a: 60 times larger
w: √60 ≈ 7.7 times larger
3600 times larger
Equal, with higher tip speed
questions.x: Ideal power P = T^{3/2}/√(2ρA) depends on the product ρA, so a 60 times lower density requires 60 times the disk area.

questions.q: Same vehicle mass and disk area. Titan has 4.4× Earth's density and 0.14× its gravity. Ideal hover power on Titan is:
questions.a: About 1/40 of Earth's
w: About 1/15 of Earth's
About 1/4 of Earth's
About 1/2 of Earth's

questions.q: Human-powered aircraft (about 0.3 kW sustained) are designed with:
questions.a: Low W/S, large span, and low flight speed
w: High W/S, short span, and high flight speed
Low W/S, short span, and high flight speed
High W/S, large span, and low flight speed
questions.x: Very low wing loading allows flight at low speed, and a large span minimizes induced drag D_i = L²/(π q b² e), keeping power required within human output.

questions.q: Wing divergence is:
questions.a: Static instability: aero twist moment beats torsional stiffness
w: Dynamic coupling of bending and torsion modes with a phase lag
Loss of roll control as wing twist cancels the aileron moments
Structural shaking from separated, unsteady flow over the wings
questions.x: Divergence is a static torsional instability in which the aerodynamic twisting moment grows faster with q than the elastic restoring moment.

questions.q: Above the aileron reversal speed:
questions.a: Wing twist from the aileron reverses the roll moment
w: The wing twists without bound under static aero loads
Bending and torsion couple into a growing oscillation
Separated flow buffets the wing and the ailerons
questions.x: A down-deflected aileron twists the wing nose down, and above the reversal speed this twist outweighs the aileron lift so the roll moment changes sign.

questions.q: Flutter is best described as:
questions.a: Dynamic instability coupling bending and torsion
w: Static instability coupling bending and torsion modes
Forced vibration from separated flow at high α
Static loss of control power at high dynamic pressure
questions.x: Flutter is a dynamic, self-excited aeroelastic instability in which coupled bending and torsion modes extract energy from the airflow.

questions.q: Match each aeroelastic phenomenon to its description
pairs: Static: aero twisting moment exceeds torsional stiffness
Static: wing twist cancels the control rolling moment
questions.x: Divergence and reversal are static aeroelastic phenomena, flutter is a dynamic self-excited instability, and buffet is a forced response to separated flow.

questions.q: Put the first-pass takeoff weight sizing steps in order (Raymer style)
steps: Define the mission profile and payload
Get W_e/W_0 from trends and W_f/W_0 from segment fractions
Compare with the guess and iterate to convergence
questions.x: The mission sets the segment fractions, and because W_e/W_0 depends on W_0 the sizing equation is solved by iteration.

questions.q: Raymer's statistical trend is W_e/W_0 = A·W_0^C. For most aircraft classes, as W_0 grows, W_e/W_0:
questions.a: Decreases slowly
w: Increases slowly
Stays exactly constant
Falls in proportion to 1/W_0
questions.x: The exponent C is small and negative for most classes, so the empty weight fraction falls gently as takeoff weight rises.

questions.q: Jet cruise: R = 5000 km, V = 250 m/s, L/D = 15, TSFC c = 0.6 1/hr. The cruise weight fraction W_f/W_i is about:
A sizing carpet plot typically shows:
questions.a: W_0 over a T/W, W/S grid with constraints overlaid
w: Drag polars at each Mach number, with buffet overlaid
V-n envelopes at each altitude, with gusts overlaid
A compressor map with surge and operating lines
questions.x: A carpet plot shows sized takeoff weight across a grid of T/W and W/S with performance constraints overlaid, locating the lightest feasible design.

boards.prompt: Derive the Mattingly master equation from the energy equation and explain the physical meaning of each term.
points: Start from specific excess power: (T−D)V/W = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt
Write D = qS(K₁C_L² + K₂C_L + C_D0) with C_L = nβW_TO/(qS)
Substitute T = αT_SL and W = βW_TO, then divide by βW_TO and V
α is installed thrust lapse and β is the weight fraction at the segment
The terms are drag (parasite and induced), climb rate, and acceleration

boards.prompt: Sketch a constraint diagram for a carrier-based fighter and locate the design point.
points: Axes are T_SL/W_TO versus W_TO/S
Stall and approach speed for arrested landing give vertical lines capping W/S
Catapult launch airspeed is catapult end speed plus wind over deck
Turn, climb, and dash constraints bound the feasible region from below
The design point is at the lowest feasible T/W, at the highest W/S allowed there

boards.prompt: Sketch power required and power available versus airspeed at sea level and at altitude, and explain the key speeds.
points: Parasite power grows with V³ and induced power falls as 1/V, giving a U-shaped curve
Minimum power speed is 3^(−1/4) ≈ 0.76 times the minimum drag speed
At altitude, at the same C_L, V and P_R both scale by 1/√σ: the curve shifts up and to the right
Excess power P_A − P_R over W gives rate of climb; the high-speed intersection gives V_max

boards.prompt: An aircraft holds a level sustained turn. Derive load factor and turn radius, and tell me what limits the turn.
points: L cos φ = W and L sin φ = (W/g)V²/R give n = 1/cos φ
R = V²/(g√(n²−1)) and turn rate ω = g√(n²−1)/V
Sustained turn requires T = D at the elevated load factor, so excess thrust sets the limit
Induced drag scales with n², so tighter turns need more thrust
C_Lmax and the structural limit load factor also bound the turn

boards.prompt: Draw a V-n diagram for a transport aircraft and label every boundary.
points: Positive and negative stall curves n = ρV²SC_Lmax/(2W) on the left
Limit load lines, typically +2.5 and −1.0 for a transport
Corner speed V_A = V_S1√n_max
Cruise speed V_C and dive speed V_D, with V_D closing the envelope
Ultimate load = 1.5 × limit load

boards.prompt: How do gust loads depend on wing loading and lift-curve slope, and why does that matter for a light, high aspect ratio aircraft?
points: Δn = ρ₀U_de V_e a K_g/(2W/S) in EAS form
Δn grows with lift-curve slope a and EAS, and scales as 1/(W/S)
K_g is the gust alleviation factor, a function of the mass ratio
High aspect ratio raises a, and low W/S raises Δn, so gust lines can set the envelope

boards.prompt: Sketch the ideal Brayton cycle on T-s and p-v diagrams with station numbers, and tell me what the enclosed area means.
points: Compression 2→3 and expansion 4→9 are isentropic: vertical lines on T-s
Heat addition 3→4 and heat rejection are isobaric: constant pressure lines diverging with s
Along an isobar dh = T ds, so heat added equals the enthalpy rise
The enclosed area on either diagram equals net work per unit mass
Ideal thermal efficiency is 1 − 1/π^((γ−1)/γ), rising with overall pressure ratio π; T_t4 caps the cycle top

boards.prompt: Compare an afterburning turbojet with a high bypass turbofan for thrust and efficiency.
points: Thrust F = ṁ(V_e − V_0) + (p_e − p_0)A_e
η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V_0) rises as exhaust velocity approaches flight speed
High bypass moves a large mass flow with a small velocity increment, giving high η_p and low TSFC
An afterburner burns fuel downstream of the turbine, raising V_e and thrust at a large rise in fuel flow and TSFC

boards.prompt: Draw the lift distribution on a finite wing, show the tip vortices, and explain where induced drag comes from.
points: Bound circulation Γ(y) sheds trailing vorticity dΓ/dy that rolls up into tip vortices
Trailing vortices induce downwash, tilting the local lift vector back to create induced drag
Kutta-Joukowski gives sectional lift L' = ρ∞V∞Γ
C_Di = C_L²/(π e AR) with AR = b²/S
Elliptic loading gives uniform downwash and minimum induced drag for a given span, e = 1

boards.prompt: Explain the drag polar and the difference between C_D0 and parasite drag force.
points: C_D = C_D0 + KC_L² with K = 1/(π e AR) and Oswald efficiency e
C_D0 is the zero-lift drag coefficient from skin friction, form, and interference drag
Parasite drag force qSC_D0 grows with dynamic pressure and reference area
Induced drag force D_i = L²/(π q b² e) depends on span loading and falls as q rises
Above M_dd, wave drag adds a sharp rise in C_D

boards.prompt: Derive hover power from momentum theory and explain the role of disk loading.
points: Actuator disk: far wake velocity is 2v_i, so T = 2ρA v_i²
v_i = √(T/(2ρA)) and ideal power P = T v_i = T^{3/2}/√(2ρA)
Power per unit thrust P/T = √((T/A)/(2ρ)) grows with disk loading T/A
Figure of merit = ideal power / actual power, about 0.7 to 0.8 for good rotors

boards.prompt: Why is a tiltrotor a compromise, and how would you size a rotorcraft for Mars or for Titan?
points: Low disk loading favors hover efficiency; high propeller efficiency at speed favors cruise
Tiltrotor proprotors use intermediate disk loading, trading hover figure of merit for cruise speed and range
Mars low density raises v_i and power at fixed area, so designs use large rotors, with tip Mach number limiting rotor speed
Titan's dense atmosphere and low gravity cut ideal hover power sharply, since P ∝ T^{3/2}/√ρ

boards.prompt: Distinguish divergence, aileron reversal, flutter, and buffet, and explain how speed and stiffness enter each.
points: Divergence: static torsional instability where the aero twisting moment overcomes torsional stiffness
Higher torsional stiffness and a smaller offset between aerodynamic center and elastic axis raise divergence speed
Aileron reversal: wing twist from control deflection cancels the rolling moment above the reversal speed
Flutter: dynamic self-excited coupling of bending and torsion that extracts energy from the airflow
Buffet: forced vibration from separated, unsteady flow at high C_L or from transonic shock motion

boards.prompt: Walk me through the aircraft sizing loop from mission definition to takeoff weight.
points: Define the mission profile and break it into segments with weight fractions
Cruise and loiter fractions come from Breguet: exp(−Rc/(V L/D)) and exp(−Ec/(L/D))
Empty weight fraction comes from statistical trends that fall slowly with W_0
W_0 = (W_crew + W_payload)/(1 − W_f/W_0 − W_e/W_0), solved iteratively
Constraint analysis sets T/W and W/S; carpet plots show the W_0 optimum within constraints
